clinicalPearls: Hemolytic anemia (HA) is anemia from increased red-cell destruction with a normal (usually increased) marrow supply; unlike acute blood loss, cells are destroyed within the body rather than physically lost (p.791).

Classify by primary etiology (inherited vs acquired), tempo (acute vs chronic), severity, site of hemolysis (intravascular vs extravascular), and mechanism (intracorpuscular vs extracorpuscular defects) (p.791, Table 105-1).

Inherited HA generally reflects intracorpuscular defects (hemoglobinopathies, enzymopathies such as G6PD, membrane-cytoskeleton defects); acquired HA generally reflects extracorpuscular factors (autoimmune, microangiopathic/mechanical, toxins, drugs, infection). Exceptions: PNH (inherited-like somatic mutation but acquired) and familial/atypical HUS (p.791-792, Table 105-1).

Core clinical sign is jaundice; patients may report dark urine; splenomegaly is common as a preferential site of hemolysis, the liver may enlarge, and pigment gallstones are common with chronic hemolysis (p.791).

Laboratory hallmarks: increased reticulocytes (both percentage and the more definitive absolute count), raised MCV with macrocytes/polychromasia on smear, increased unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin and AST, raised LDH, and reduced-to-absent haptoglobin (p.791, Table 105-2).

Extravascular hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen; intravascular hemolysis is signalled by hemoglobinuria (often with hemosiderinuria), free plasma hemoglobin, markedly raised LDH (up to ~10x), and low haptoglobin, with bilirubin only mildly elevated (p.791, Table 105-2).

A positive broad-spectrum direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is on its own almost diagnostic of autoimmune HA; the broad reagent detects bound immunoglobulin and/or complement (C3 fragments) on red cells (p.801).

Warm AIHA (mostly IgG, optimal 37C) causes predominantly extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes; cold agglutinin disease (mostly IgM anti-I, optimal 4-30C) activates complement causing intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria plus Kupffer-cell extravascular destruction in the liver (p.801-803, Fig. 105-9, Table 105-8).

Compensated hemolysis: a brisk EPO-driven erythropoietic response can fully offset red-cell destruction so an inherited hemolytic condition may present without anemia; it can decompensate in pregnancy, folate deficiency, or renal failure (p.792).
harrison.pathophysiology: The mature red cell loses mitochondria and ribosomes, leaving anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway) as the sole source of ATP and the hexose-monophosphate shunt (via G6PD-generated NADPH and reduced glutathione) as defense against oxidant stress; damaged proteins cannot be replaced, so any metabolic failure ultimately damages the membrane or the cation pump and shortens the ~120-day life span. Senescent or damaged red cells expose band-3 neoantigens, become opsonized, and are phagocytosed by splenic, hepatic, and other macrophages (extravascular hemolysis); this senescence process is accelerated in many HAs. The essential common feature is increased red-cell turnover; when destruction outpaces marrow production, anemia results. Chronic intravascular hemolysis causes iron loss via hemoglobinuria, whereas chronic extravascular hemolysis (especially if transfused) tends toward iron overload and, untreated, secondary hemochromatosis (p.791-792).
additionalDifferentials: Inherited intracorpuscular defects: hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassemia; Chap. 103), enzymopathies (G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency, pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase deficiency), membrane-cytoskeleton defects (hereditary spherocytosis) (p.791-792, Table 105-1)

Acquired extracorpuscular causes: autoimmune (warm AIHA, cold agglutinin disease, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria), microangiopathic/mechanical (prosthetic valve, march hemoglobinuria), paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, toxic/drug-induced, infectious (p.792, 801-804, Table 105-1)
Familial (atypical) hemolytic-uremic syndrome from inherited dysregulation permitting excessive complement activation (p.799-800)
infectionMimics: Malaria - the most frequent infectious cause of HA in endemic areas (p.801)
Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 causing HUS, more common in children (p.801)
Clostridium perfringens sepsis - life-threatening intravascular hemolysis from lecithinase toxin (open wounds, septic abortion, contaminated blood unit) (p.801, Table 105-7)
Babesia, and Mycoplasma infection (associated with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria); viral triggers (EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19, HIV, HCV) of secondary autoimmune HA (p.801-802, Table 105-8)
nonInfectiousMimics: Compensated hemolysis presenting without anemia, mimicking a non-hemolytic state until it decompensates (p.792)
Reticulocytosis-driven macrocytosis that can be mistaken for a megaloblastic process (p.791)
Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis causing a precipitous hemoglobin fall in a chronic hemolytic patient, mimicking acute worsening of hemolysis (p.792)
Coombs-negative AIHA, which can still be severe when a high-affinity antibody opsonizes red cells with few molecules (p.802)
additionalInvestigations: Reticulocyte count - corrected percentage and absolute count (often neglected in initial anemia workup) (p.791)
Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, AST, LDH, haptoglobin (p.791, Table 105-2)
Urine for hemoglobinuria/hemosiderinuria and stool/urine urobilinogen when intravascular hemolysis suspected (p.791)
Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes (microangiopathy/fragmentation), spherocytes (AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis), bite cells (G6PD), basophilic stippling (lead/P5N deficiency) (p.799-804)
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test - broad-spectrum then specific anti-Ig/anti-C reagents (p.801)
Quantitative G6PD assay (screening tests can miss deficiency soon after a hemolytic attack because young high-G6PD reticulocytes mask it); DNA testing and point-of-care tests available (p.799-800)
Flow cytometry for CD59-negative red cell population in PNH (p.801, Table 105-7)
Donath-Landsteiner antibody for paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria; blood cultures for clostridial septicemia (p.801, Table 105-7)
Red cell survival study (51Cr or nonradioactive 15N) as the gold standard for shortened life span; bone marrow (if done) shows erythroid hyperplasia, usually not required (p.791-792)
redFlags: Schistocytes (fragmented/helmet cells) on smear indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) - consider TTP, HUS, and DIC; an emergency requiring urgent evaluation (p.799, 801, Table 105-7)
Abrupt severe drop in hemoglobin (to as low as 4 g/dL within days) in warm AIHA with jaundice and splenomegaly - a medical emergency (p.801)
Acute renal failure - the most serious threat from acute hemolytic attacks in adults (e.g., G6PD-related), and a predictor of poor AIHA outcome (p.799, 801)
Hemoglobinuria signalling intravascular hemolysis (mismatched transfusion, PNH, clostridial sepsis, march hemoglobinuria, favism) (p.801, Table 105-7)
Evans syndrome (AIHA plus autoimmune thrombocytopenia) signals high-risk disease and may indicate underlying immune deficiency (p.801)
Mismatched (usually ABO-incompatible) blood transfusion causing abrupt intravascular hemolysis (p.801, Table 105-7)
Clostridium perfringens sepsis causing life-threatening intravascular hemolysis (p.801)
harrison.prognosis: Transient hemolysis usually has no long-term consequences beyond increased erythropoietic (folate) requirement; recurrent or persistent hemolysis predisposes to pigment gallstones, splenomegaly with hypersplenism (neutropenia/thrombocytopenia), and, with chronic extravascular hemolysis or repeated transfusion, iron overload progressing to secondary hemochromatosis affecting liver and heart. Warm AIHA carries ~5-10% mortality even with appropriate management; predictors of worse outcome/relapse include Evans syndrome, hemoglobin <6 g/dL, acute renal failure, infection, and high-affinity antibody. G6PD-related acute hemolysis generally resolves fully once the trigger is removed and in the absence of comorbidity, with full recovery from renal failure the rule when there is no prior kidney disease (p.792, 799, 801).
pitfalls: Neglecting the reticulocyte count, a key early clue to a hemolytic mechanism (p.791)

Screening (semiquantitative) G6PD tests give falsely normal results immediately after a hemolytic attack because the oldest deficient cells are destroyed and young reticulocytes have higher G6PD - use a quantitative assay; female heterozygotes may also be missed (p.799-800)

Dismissing Coombs-negative AIHA as not serious - high-affinity antibody can cause severe disease with few bound molecules; false-positive Coombs can follow transfusion, organ transplant, or Ig/anti-lymphocyte products (p.801-802)
Assuming an inherited hemolytic disorder always causes anemia - compensated hemolysis can be normo-hemoglobinemic until decompensation (p.792)

In cold agglutinin disease, prednisone and splenectomy are ineffective (unlike warm AIHA), and transfused (I-positive) red cells survive no longer than the patient's; the blood bag and patient extremities must be kept warm (p.803)
Misattributing favism to fava bean pollen inhalation (it does not cause favism) or to other beans (which are safe) (p.799)
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal grading. Severity is gauged clinically by the hemoglobin level and tempo (mild compensated hemolysis without anemia through to abrupt severe drops to ~4 g/dL in AIHA) and by the site of hemolysis: intravascular hemolysis is signalled by hemoglobinuria, free plasma hemoglobin, LDH up to ~10x normal, and absent haptoglobin, whereas extravascular hemolysis chiefly raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen. High-risk markers in AIHA include hemoglobin <6 g/dL, acute renal failure, infection, and Evans syndrome (p.791-792, 801, Tables 105-2, 105-7).
